did.abstract: Jim Toy was an LGBTQ+ activist and is one of the first gay men to publicly come out in the state of Michigan. Toy was heavily involved in a number of activist groups, including the Gay Liberation Front (in Detroit and Ann Arbor); the Huron Valley Chapter of Wellness Network (now the HIV/AIDS Resource Center); the OutLoud Chorus; the Oasis TBLG Outreach Ministries of the Episcopal Diocese of Michigan; the Transgender Advocacy Project (TAP); the Inclusive Justice/Together in Faith coalition in Michigan; and the Washtenaw Rainbow Action Project (WRAP), now known as the Jim Toy Community Center. His papers document his activist work at the University of Michigan, in the Episcopal church, and across the state, as well as his personal correspondence. This collection features Toy's records from his work with the Spectrum Center, which he helped found in 1971, and where he worked until 1994, as well as his work with the Affirmative Action Office. It also features his personal papers, materials from his extensive work as an LGBTQ+ advocate, and his personal and professional correspondence.
did.langmaterial: The materials are primarily in English, with some materials in French, and a small portion of materials in Japanese.

p.emph: Access Restrictions for University of Michigan Records

blockquote.p: University records are public records and once fully processed are generally open to research use. Records that contain personally identifiable information will be restricted in order to protect individual privacy. Certain administrative records are restricted in accordance with university policy as outlined below. The restriction of university records is subject to compliance with applicable laws, including the Michigan Freedom of Information Act.

Categories of Restricted Records
Patient/client records are restricted for one-hundred (100) years from the date of their creation. The terms of use for particular records older than 100 years may require the research to sign a Patient/Client Access Agreement.
Executive records: Records generated by the university's executive officers, deans, directors, department heads, and their designated support staff are restricted for twenty (20) years from the date of their creation.
Restricted files are indicated in the contents list of the collection’s finding aid with a restriction note indicating the restriction type and the date of expiration.

For further information on the restriction policy and placing Freedom of Information Act requests for restricted material, consult the reference archivist at the Bentley Historical Library (bentley.ref@umich.edu) or the University of Michigan Freedom of Information Office website (https://foia.vpcomm.umich.edu/).

acqinfo.p: The collection was received from James Toy (donor no. 8504) in several accessions during the summer of 1996. Additions were received in 1997, 2008, 2012, 2013, and 2019.
Additional materials were received from the Office of University Human Resources (donor no. 5818) in July 2010.

arrangement.p: The James W. Toy papers are arranged into six series: (1) Personal papers, (2) University Career, (3) Advocacy and Outreach, (4) Religion, (5) Correspondence, and (6) Topical files.

bioghist.p: James Willis Toy, known as Jim Toy, was born in New York City on April 29, 1930, to James Toy, a Chinese man born in Portland, Oregon, and Imogen Hamblen Toy, a Scotch-Irish woman who was born in Japan. His mother passed away shortly after he was born, so early in Jim Toy's life, his father moved the family to Granville, Ohio to be closer to his maternal grandparents. In 1933, James Toy Sr. remarried, and Ruth Rickett Toy became Jim's stepmother.

Jim Toy graduated from Granville High School in 1947, and following graduation, enrolled in Denison University in Granville, Ohio. In 1951, Jim Toy graduated from Denison University with a Bachelor of Arts in French and Music and accepted a position teaching English in France. He lived near Bordeaux and in Corsica until 1953 when he moved to New York where he worked in a hospital blood bank to fulfill a conscientious-objector requirement in lieu of military service. In 1957, he moved to Detroit where he became organist-choirmaster at St. Joseph's Episcopal Church. Through St. Joseph's choir, Toy met Janet Barnes, whom he married one year later in 1958. Soon after, in 1960, Toy enrolled in the musicology program at the University of Michigan; while he achieved doctoral candidacy, he did not complete a dissertation, therefore not completing the degree.

According to Toy, the 1960s was the period in which he struggled with concerns about his sexuality, resulting in his divorce in 1963. In April of 1970, Toy came out publicly as a gay man at an anti-war rally in Detroit. He was one of the first people in Michigan to come out of the closet in a public forum. That same year, Toy helped to found and serve as secretary of both the Detroit Gay Liberation Movement (later known as the Detroit Gay Liberation Front) and the Ann Arbor Gay Liberation Front, both organizations established to advocate for LGBTQ+ civil rights.

In the summer of 1970, the Gay Liberation Front (GLF) attempted to hold a conference at the University of Michigan where "gay people in the Midwest could gather to discuss Queer issues" (Shabelski and Code, 2025). President Fleming denied this request because it was not "educational in character" (Shabelski and Code, 2025). While a small conference was held in the Student Activities Center, Toy (among other activists) advocated for a program to address the needs of LGBTQ+ students. In 1971, the university, under its Office of Special Services and Programs, created a "Human Sexuality Office" (now known as the Spectrum Center) with two quarter-time employees (one lesbian and one gay-male advocate). Toy became the university's first gay male advocate.

In his capacity as the gay-male advocate - and alongside lesbian advocate, Cynthia Gair - Toy stated the Spectrum Center's charge was "to help educate the University community and the community-at-large about the nature of sexuality and, specifically, homosexuality; about the oppression that people endure; and about the rights that gay people should enjoy" (Human Sexuality Office Annual Report, 1971). As such, the center established education programs, peer advising and counseling, and advocacy projects to advance the needs of the LGBTQ+ community on- and off-campus. The office also served as a clearinghouse where gay men and lesbians could go for information about gay life and activities. In addition, they hosted the GLF operation and funded "Gay Hotline" to provide additional crisis support for LGBTQ+ folks.

Beginning in 1972, Toy and his colleagues worked to amend Regental Bylaw (RB) 14.06 to specifically prohibit discrimination based upon an individual's sexual orientation at the university. President Shapiro issued a Presidential Policy on non-discrimination in 1984 (RB 14.06 would not include sexual orientation until 1993) in response to campus protests, and established the President's Task Force on Sexual Orientation. Both Toy and Gair were included on the task force. In 1987, with a reorganization of the office and the appointment of Billie Edwards as director, the advocate positions became co-coordinators and Toy was made a full-time employee.

Toy earned his Master's degree in clinical social work in 1981 while also organizing and teaching the course "Gay Issues in Social Work" at the U-M School of Social Work. Throughout his career, he continued teaching and facilitating training sessions both at the University of Michigan and at other universities, churches, and social organizations. In 1994, following an administrative reorganization at the newly-renamed Lesbian Gay Bisexual Programs Office (LGBPO) at the University of Michigan, Jim Toy was reassigned to the university's Affirmative Action office as an Affirmative Action Representative. Still, he continued advocating for LGBTQ+ people, assisting with workplace transition support for transgender employees in the early 2000's and highlighting the unique experiences and needs of bisexual people. In 2001, Toy, along with LGBTA Office Director Frederic MacDonald-Dennis and sexologist and professor at the University of Michigan School of Medicine, Dr. Sandra Cole, advocated for the inclusion of gender identity for which discrimination is prohibited to RB 14.06. This led to the creation of the Provost's Task Force on LGBT Campus Climate (2003) and, eventually, the addition of gender identity and expression as protected classes to RB 14.06 in 2007.

In 1999, Toy was invited to become an honorary member of the Order of Angell, then known as Michigamua, as an advisor. In Toy's words, he accepted the invitation to "help effect change within that organization" (Toy 2007). The organization was well known on campus as appropriating Indigenous cultures; in 2002, the Students of Color Coalition took over the tower of Michigan Union to protest that exploitation. Toy received criticism from students regarding his membership in the secret society.

Toy's activism on behalf of LGBTQ+ civil rights extended beyond the university. He was on the committee that drafted an anti-discrimination ordinance for the city of Ann Arbor, adopted in July 1972. That same year he co-authored a Gay Pride Week proclamation subsequently approved by the city council of Ann Arbor. On the state level, Toy served as a member of the Task Force on the Family and Sexuality of the Civil Rights Committee of the Michigan State House of Representatives. In addition, he continued to work as a community counselor and therapist, providing pro bono service to help individuals, couples, and groups address concerns of sexual orientation and of HIV/AIDS. A large portion of Toy's activist work focused on working with religious organizations, particularly in American Christianity, on how to create inclusive spaces for LGBTQ+ people, both within and outside the church. Other organizations in which Toy participated included the local chapter of the ACLU, the state board of the Michigan Organization for Human Rights, the Ann Arbor Area Association for Civil Concerns, the Lesbian/Gay Political Caucus of Washtenaw County, and the Huron Valley Chapter of Wellness Network (now the HIV/AIDS Resource Center, or HARC).
Jim Toy passed away at the age of 91 on January 1, 2022.

scopecontent.p: The James W. Toy papers are organized into six series: Personal Papers, University Career, Advocacy and Outreach, Religion, Topical Files, and Correspondence.

The Personal Papers series covers Toy's biographical materials, photographs, family history, school records, and personal writings including poetry, speeches, and notes. Also included are his appointment books, materials from Toy's time in France, and drafts of musical arrangements.

The University Career series is separated into three sub-series: Spectrum Center/LGMPO, Office of Equity and Diversity, and Other University of Michigan Work. The Spectrum Center/LGMPO sub-series covers materials from the entire history of the Spectrum Center at the University of Michigan, with a particular focus on the Lesbian-Gay Male Programs Office. This includes administrative records, operational materials for the Gay Male hotline, event materials, and LGBTQ+ resources. The Office of Equity and Diversity series covers Toy's employment at what was then known as the HR Affirmative Action office. This includes diversity workshop materials, advising, and gender transition-in-the-workplace workshops. Materials in the Other University of Michigan Work sub-series cover conferences, school of social work courses, and community workshops Toy conducted during his time at the University.

The Activism and Outreach series covers Toy's activities as a LGBTQ+ activist in Michigan and documents the activities of many LGBTQ+ political groups. These include: the Gay Liberation Front, PFLAG (also known as Parents and Friends of Lesbians and Gays), Equality Michigan (previously the Triangle Foundation and Michigan Equality), The Peninsula Group, GLSEN (also known as the Gay, Lesbian, and Straight Education Network), Washtenaw Rainbow Action Project, and several other local LGBTQ+ networks. Also included in this series are materials related to several HIV/AIDS organizations that Toy was involved in, particularly in Washtenaw County, as well as the OutLoud Chorus.

The Religion series covers all of Toy's involvement with religion, particularly the Episcopal Church. This includes OASIS ministries, as well as LGBTQ+ issues in the Episcopal Church. It also includes his involvement with some Unitarian Universalist organizations and documents LGBTQ+ issues in American Christianity generally.

Topical Files consists mainly of subject files, collected or created by Jim Toy, and relating to his involvement with or mentoring of other gay organizations. Organizations represented with significant amounts of material include the Gay Hotline, the Gay Liberation Front, the Gay Community Services, LaGROC, the Committee on Lesbian and Gay Concerns, and the Michigan Organization for Human Rights. A collection of LGBTQ+ publications collected by Toy are also represented in this series, as well as collected event materials. Of note is a long run of Sean's Triangle News, an email newsletter documented in print outs and in Toy's email inboxes.

The Correspondence series covers all of Jim Toy's correspondence: personal and family letters, work correspondence, and correspondence related to Toy's church involvement. It also includes correspondence with incarcerated and formerly incarcerated individuals, some as part of Toy's work with the American Friends Service Committee.

userestrict.p: Donor(s) have transferred any applicable copyright to the Regents of the University of Michigan but the collection may contain third-party materials for which copyright was not transferred. Patrons are responsible for determining the appropriate use or reuse of materials.

relatedmaterial.p: The Bentley Historical Library houses the following related collections: the Spectrum Center (University of Michigan) records, Billie Louise Edwards Papers, Sandra S. Cole papers and the Washtenaw Rainbow Action Project Records.

processinfo.p: The James W. Toy papers were processed by: Thomas E. Powers and Rachel Erlich in 1996-1997; Marc Levitt in 2008; Cherie Edmonds in 2013; Tara Bell in 2014; Elizabeth Hannigan in 2019; and Gideon Goodrich, Alexis Miettinen, Aubrey Lockwood, and Marc Tsuno in 2025. This finding aid contains original creator-supplied titles where available. Original folder titles have been maintained to preserve the original context of how the creator labeled their files; they may include outdated or harmful descriptive language, particularly regarding LGBTQ+ communities in Michigan. Due to the sensitive nature of the counseling records and some of the transgender transition-in-the-workplace workshops, names of individuals have been removed from the finding aid; some names are still included on folder titles.

A note on archival description: Due to the evolving language surrounding the LGBTQIA+ community, Gideon Goodrich and Alexis Miettinen chose to use the umbrella term LGBTQ+ (as used by the Homosaurus international vocabulary of LGBTQ+ terms). Other common terms - such as LGBT, queer, gay, 2SLGBTQ+, and GLBT - are contextually appropriate when describing communities. In addition, Jim Toy preferred an alternative acronym - TBLG - ordering members of his community in order from (in his opinion) communities needing the most to least civil rights support. However, in order to best represent Toy's work as an activist, Gideon Goodrich and Alexis Miettinen chose to use LGBTQ+ throughout the finding aid.

accruals.p: No further additions to the records are expected.

scopecontent.p: This sub-series represents materials from Jim Toy's work with what is now known as the Spectrum Center. It should be noted that Toy left the center while it was still known as the Lesbian-Gay-Bisexual Programs Office. The finding aid refers to the Spectrum Center by its current name (as of writing in 2025) - it has also been known as the Human Sexuality Office, the Lesbian and Gay Male Programs Office, the Lesbian Gay Bisexual Programs Office, the LGBT Resource Center, and the Office of LGBT Affairs.

The Lesbian Gay Male Bisexual Programs Office sub-series consists of records generated by Jim Toy (with some records of the lesbian advocate) in his capacity as gay male advocate within the Human Sexuality Office (and successor units) of the University of Michigan. These records relate to the administration of the office, its programs, and to its relationship with the larger university community. As Toy held this position for twenty-three years while the position of lesbian advocate was filled by a number of different individuals, the files reflect more the work of the gay male advocate and less the activities of the lesbian advocate. Of special note are those files pertaining to the effort to revise the U-M Regental Bylaw 14.06 and thus provide protection against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, the work of the Task Force on Sexual Orientation, and the drafting of the two policy statements on discrimination and discriminatory harassment (for students, and for faculty and staff).

scopecontent.p: The Office of Equity and Diversity series contains materials from Jim Toy's time working with a sub-unit of the Office of Human Resources and Affirmative Action. The series features correspondence, meeting minutes, reports, and surveys from Toy's participation in a School of Social Work task force about the climate for Transgender, Bisexual, Lesbian, and Gay (TBLG) students, faculty, and staff. The series also contains committee reports from the University of Michigan's Task Force on Campus Climate for TBLG students and materials about university policies on gender identity and inclusion.

scopecontent.p: The Peninsula Group (TPG) was formed by a concerned group of LGBT community leaders following the passage of Proposal 2 (Michigan's Constitutional ban on same-sex marriage) in November 2004. It was believed that Michigan needed an LGBT think-tank, using proven strategic planning techniques, so that the collective LGBT community could move forward in a proactive manner to secure equal rights for all. Integral to the strategic planning of the Peninsula Group was a statewide survey in which over 2000 respondents participated. Members of the Peninsula Group informed, facilitated, listened to, made note of, encouraged, and guided attendees to a consensus. It was agreed that the next step was for several members of the strategic planning team, formally known as the Peninsula Group, to form a Design Team for the proposed Michigan Association of LGBT Organizations.

The Michigan Association for LGBT and Ally Organizations began operating in 2007. Records include plans for hiring a Project Manager to oversee operations, presentations by the Design Team which outline the purpose of the organization, grant applications, and other project files. The series also contains records related to a summit held at Central Michigan University in 2008 including presentations and evaluations of the Summit.
